priorInvolvementDisclosure: I returned ACCEPT on v16 at 0/0. Codex returned REJECT with two SHOULD-FIX findings. Having read both, Codex is right and I was wrong; this is my fourth under-call in this lineage and the first where I certified clean an artifact that was not. The two misses share one cause, and it is method rather than attention. On HAE16-CX-01 I executed the artifact's coverage rule, reported zero missing, and never asked whether the rule encoded a sound obligation. honestyRepairsFromVN is defined as findings repaired in a successor, so forcing nineteen ADVISORY-NON-BLOCKING ids into it classified unrepaired standing observations as repairs. I did worse than miss it: I saw the or-to-and edit and praised it in my v16 verdict as closing the same class of weakening as the FC-ROUND-TRIP defect, when it was the edit that created the false classification. On HAE16-CX-02 I wrote a per-lane comparison in my own script, found it passed, and reported the rule verified, when the rule as written compared only set unions; my script was stronger than the rule, so I validated the data and not the rule. I also had the decisive evidence for Codex's extractor point in hand at v14, when the frozen v10 Claude file's integer counters plus combined findings[] crashed my parser and I silently branched around it, treating undocumented schema variance as my tooling problem rather than an artifact under-specification. The corrected method I committed to in my stub, before looking at v17, was to test what each governing rule permits by constructing counterexamples rather than checking that today's data conforms, to re-run Codex's two counterexamples against the new check, to verify the extractor against both schemas actually present in the corpus, and to treat friction in my own tooling as a candidate finding. All four were carried out and are recorded below. One further guard: having been wrong in the lenient direction at v16, the temptation is to reject here to compensate. That would be as wrong as the original error. The verdict below tracks this artifact's evidence.

advisories.title: Three advisory subjects remain substantively unaddressed from v11 through v17
advisories.observation: FC-SUBTYPE-CLASS still exercises no CA-3 row, though CA-3 carries the largest subtype domain including the deferred KEYCHAIN. destinations.actionSubtype still reads 'Required for CA-1, CA-3, CA-4-HOST' followed by the serialized restatement 'on CA-1/CA-3/CA-4'. coveredActs still keys the host classes as CA-1-host-head and CA-4-host against the record vocabulary CA-1-HOST-HEAD and CA-4-HOST. Both reviewers have raised all three independently across six generations, most recently as HAE16-ADV-01/02/03, all correctly registered ADVISORY-NON-BLOCKING and correctly absent from the repair arrays.
advisories.whyNotShouldFix: The merits are unchanged. The subtype-to-class binding is stated normatively in three independent places, the record perClassMap over all four record literals, the serialized per-class lists over CA-1 to CA-4, and unmatchedSerializedClass which enumerates CA-3's domain inline; only the fixture population is short. The mapping sentence is immediately restated unambiguously. The coveredActs keys are section labels, not discriminator literals. I declined to escalate at v13, v15 and v16 on these grounds and the artifact has not changed in a way that alters consequence.
advisories.suggestedDisposition: Optional. One CA-3 accept row and one CA-3 cross-class refuse row would close the first at negligible cost.

advisories.title: The id-extraction rule shares a key prefix with the repair arrays it governs, which a prefix-matching implementation of the mechanical check will mis-ingest
advisories.observation: The eight repair arrays are named honestyRepairsFromV9 through honestyRepairsFromV16, and the rule object governing their id extraction is named honestyRepairsFromVnIdExtraction, in the same top-level namespace. An implementation that enumerates the arrays by the natural prefix honestyRepairsFrom ingests the rule object as if it were a ninth repair array and reads its status, rule and appliesTo values as repair entries. I am reporting this because it happened to me: my first pass reported three FromVN prefixes that were not REPAIRED register findings, and the three were status, rule and appliesTo. Anchoring the match to honestyRepairsFromV followed by digits resolves it, and the corrected count is an exact 27 to 27 correspondence.
advisories.whyNotShouldFix: The artifact's own text is precise enough to disambiguate, since honestyRepairsFromVN is explicitly parameterised by a version number, and a correct implementation matches the digits. No data is wrong and no claim the artifact makes is false. It is a robustness hazard in a namespace the artifact leans on for mechanical enforcement, not a defect in the enforcement's result. Raised under the discipline I committed to this round, that friction in my own tooling should be surfaced as a candidate finding rather than silently worked around, which is precisely what I failed to do with the same class of evidence at v14.
advisories.suggestedDisposition: Optional. Either anchor the extraction rule's stated match to honestyRepairsFromV[0-9]+, or rename the rule object out of that prefix, for example to fromVnIdExtractionRule.

verdictBasis: The dispatch permits ACCEPT only at 0 blockers and 0 SHOULD-FIX. This review returns 0 blockers and 0 SHOULD-FIX, so the verdict is ACCEPT, and it rests on the method whose absence caused my v16 error rather than on conformance checking. Both Codex findings are repaired and each was verified against the failure mode that produced it. For HAE16-CX-01 I checked the rule's semantics rather than only the data: the repair-array definition is now scoped to REPAIRED dispositions, both inclusion and exclusion are stated, and there are exactly 27 repair entries against exactly 27 REPAIRED ids with zero advisories present, my own v16 advisory correctly excluded. For HAE16-CX-02 I implemented laneCheck, pairCheck and the extractor exactly as written, deliberately weaker than the script I wrote at v16, ran the corpus for 50 lane-id pairs matching in both directions with no duplicates, and then ran Codex's two frozen counterexamples, both of which the repaired rule now rejects. The extractor handles the two schemas that had previously broken my own parser, which was the evidence I misattributed at v14. Custody is clean on every pin, all 52 recorded inputs reproduce, the D-032 section reproduces, no prior repair regressed, and the v16 split verdict is recorded faithfully. I probed the new rules for the same under-specification class Codex twice found and record both candidates I considered; neither produces a live misclassification or a false claim. Two advisories are recorded, including one arising from friction in my own tooling that I would previously have worked around silently.
